title: Jeremiah 29:1–14
context: Jeremiah the prophet sends a letter from Jerusalem to the residue of the elders of the captivity, and to the priests, the prophets, and all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon, after Jeconiah, the queen mother, the eunuchs, the princes, the craftsmen, and the smiths had departed. The letter is carried by Elasah the son of Shaphan and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, whom Zedekiah sent to Babylon. The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, tells the captives to build houses, dwell in them, plant gardens, take wives, and multiply, and to seek the peace of the city where he has caused them to be carried, and to pray to the LORD for it, for in its peace they will have peace. They are not to let prophets and diviners deceive them, or to listen to dreams they cause to be dreamed; those voices prophesy falsely, and the LORD has not sent them. After seventy years are accomplished for Babylon, the LORD will visit them, perform his good word, and cause them to return. The LORD knows the thoughts he thinks toward them, thoughts of peace and not of evil, to give them hope and a future. They shall call, pray, and be heard; they shall seek and find him when they search with all their heart, and he will gather them and bring them again to the place from which they were carried. The seventy years and the thoughts of peace are the LORD’s word to these exiles in Babylon, about a real term of captivity and a promised return. They are not a modern personal slogan; that can be said quietly, without scolding anyone who has loved the lines. How the seventy years are reckoned—from which event, and to which return—should be hedged. Daniel 9:2, 2 Chronicles 36:21, and Ezra 1:1 may be named by reference without being blended into one scheme, as may 2 Kings 24–25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52. The names and dates of the exiles and of the two messengers may likewise be hedged. On the promise to listen when they pray, the existing box at Joshua 10:14 may be consulted.

verses.text: Now these are the words of the letter that Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the residue of the elders of the captivity, and to the priests, to the prophets, and to all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away captive from Jerusalem to Babylon,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now these are the words of the letter that Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the residue of the elders of the captivity, and to the priests, to the prophets, and to all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away captive from Jerusalem to Babylon,” The unit is a letter, sent by Jeremiah from Jerusalem to the community already in Babylon: elders, priests, prophets, and all the people of that captivity. The heading is incomplete without the next verses, which name the occasion and the carriers.

Arminian readers take the letter as a real word dispatched to real captives, who are addressed as a people who can hear and live by what is written.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also receive a historical letter from Jeremiah in Jerusalem to the residue of the Babylon captivity, in all its named ranks.

Shared ground: the audience is the exiles in Babylon, not a later reader first of all. Identities within “the residue of the elders” need not be specified beyond the text.

verses.text: (after Jeconiah the king, the queen mother, the eunuchs, the princes of Judah and Jerusalem, the craftsmen, and the smiths had departed from Jerusalem),
verses.arminianNotes:
The letter is dated after “Jeconiah the king, the queen mother, the eunuchs, the princes of Judah and Jerusalem, the craftsmen, and the smiths had departed from Jerusalem” The list marks the carrying-away already past. 2 Kings 24 tells of such a departure; the accounts should be named without being blended, and the identifications—Jeconiah often being read with the Jehoiachin of that narrative—and the exact year may be hedged.

Arminian readers take the parenthesis as the letter’s historical horizon: these people have already left, and the word that follows is for those now in Babylon, not a general essay about any hardship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read a named deportation as the setting, with king, queen mother, officials, craftsmen, and smiths already gone from Jerusalem.

Shared ground: the letter comes after that departure. Officials and dates that the verse does not explain should be left modest.

verses.text: by the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, (whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent to Babylon to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon). It said:
verses.arminianNotes:
The letter is sent “by the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, (whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent to Babylon to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon).” Two named men, on a mission Zedekiah has already sent, carry the word. Their families and the exact purpose of the royal mission are not spelled out here and should be hedged; later or earlier mentions of a Shaphan or a Hilkiah are not to be forced into identity with these two.

Arminian readers hear a letter that travels by ordinary envoys, a word that can actually reach the captives because men are already going to Babylon.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same carriers as part of the book’s setting: Elasah and Gemariah, sent by Zedekiah, bear Jeremiah’s letter to the captives.

Shared ground: the path to Babylon is a royal mission already under way. The men’s further biographies need not be invented.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says to all the captives whom I have caused to be carried away captive from Jerusalem to Babylon:
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says to all the captives whom I have caused to be carried away captive from Jerusalem to Babylon:” The letter’s voice is the LORD’s, addressed to all those captives. The LORD himself says he has caused them to be carried away. The “I” is the LORD’s, not only Nebuchadnezzar’s act from the human side.

Arminian readers take the address as inclusive of the whole captive community, a word meant for them in Babylon, while still leaving room for the king of Babylon as the one who carried them, as verse 1 has said.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same heading as the LORD’s claim: he has caused this carrying-away, and he now speaks to all those captives in Babylon.

Shared ground: the letter is the LORD’s word to the exiles. The double agency of verse 1 and verse 4 can be held together without a new contrast here.

verses.text: “Build houses and dwell in them. Plant gardens and eat their fruit.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Build houses and dwell in them. Plant gardens and eat their fruit.” The first commands are ordinary and long: houses, dwelling, gardens, and fruit. The captivity is not treated as a brief halt on the road home.

Arminian readers hear a real way of life they are to take up in Babylon, a call they can obey or refuse, against the hope of a stay so short that planting would be pointless.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same commands as the LORD’s will for the exiles: settle, dwell, plant, and eat, a life measured in seasons, not in weeks.

Shared ground: the word is to settle in the land of captivity. The lines should be kept in that setting, not turned into a general motto first of all.

verses.text: Take wives and father sons and daughters. Take wives for your sons, and give your daughters to husbands, that they may bear sons and daughters. Multiply there, and don’t be diminished.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Take wives and father sons and daughters. Take wives for your sons, and give your daughters to husbands, that they may bear sons and daughters. Multiply there, and don’t be diminished.” Family and increase are commanded in the place of exile. The “there” is Babylon, and the aim is that the people not shrink away.

Arminian readers take the command to multiply as a real charge to the community, a future in the land of captivity they are to choose and build, not a pause they need not take seriously.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same instruction as the LORD’s provision for the people’s continuance: marriage, children, and increase in Babylon, so that they are not diminished.

Shared ground: the exile is long enough for a generation to be raised. The verse is pastoral and communal, not a private slogan.

verses.text: Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to the LORD for it; for in its peace you will have peace.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to the LORD for it; for in its peace you will have peace.” They are to seek the peace of Babylon itself, and to pray to the LORD for that city, because their peace is bound up with its peace. The prayer is for the place of their exile.

Arminian readers hear a real command to pray for a foreign city, an act they can perform, and a promise that their peace is tied to the peace they seek for it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same charge as the LORD’s: seek that city’s peace, pray to the LORD for it, and find their own peace in its peace, because he has caused them to be there.

Shared ground: prayer for Babylon is part of this word to the exiles. The verse is not yet 29:12–13, but it already makes prayer for the city a duty.

verses.text: For the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel says: “Don’t let your prophets who are among you and your diviners deceive you. Don’t listen to your dreams which you cause to be dreamed.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “Don’t let your prophets who are among you and your diviners deceive you. Don’t listen to your dreams which you cause to be dreamed.” In Babylon too there are prophets and diviners, and dreams the people themselves cause to be dreamed. Those voices are not to deceive them, and the dreams are not to be listened to.

Arminian readers hear a warning the captives can heed: deception is a real danger among them, including dreams they have a hand in, and they are told not to give those voices the last word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the prohibition as the LORD’s guard on the exiles: prophets, diviners, and self-caused dreams are not to lead them.

Shared ground: false hope is present in Babylon as well as in Jerusalem. The next verse will name that hope as a false prophecy in the LORD’s name.

verses.text: For they prophesy falsely to you in my name. I have not sent them,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For they prophesy falsely to you in my name. I have not sent them,” says the LORD. The deceiving voices use the LORD’s name, and he denies that he has sent them. The charge matches what was said of the Jerusalem prophets in chapter 27, now applied to those among the captives. Deuteronomy 18:20–22 may be named by reference as shared ground, without inventing a new contrast.

Arminian readers take “I have not sent them” as a verdict the exiles can trust, and as a reason to refuse words spoken in the LORD’s name that contradict the letter.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same unsent status as the LORD’s own word over the Babylon prophets and diviners: they prophesy falsely in his name, and he has not sent them.

Shared ground: the issue is a false word in the LORD’s name, not a theory of prophecy added to the chapter.

verses.text: For the LORD says, “After seventy years are accomplished for Babylon, I will visit you and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place.
verses.arminianNotes:
“After seventy years are accomplished for Babylon, I will visit you and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place.” The good word is a visit and a return, after seventy years are accomplished for Babylon. The promise belongs to these captives and to that term, not first of all to a modern private plan. How the seventy years are counted—from which event in Judah’s fall or Babylon’s rise, and to which return—should be hedged. Daniel 9:2, 2 Chronicles 36:21, and Ezra 1:1 may be named by reference without being forced into one reckoning, as may the earlier word of Jeremiah 25.

Arminian readers hear a dated hope the exiles can wait for: a real return after a real term, which also means the stay is long, as the commands to build and plant have already implied.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the seventy years as the LORD’s set term for Babylon, after which he will visit and perform his good word by causing them to return to this place.

Shared ground: the return is promised, and it is after seventy years for Babylon. The reckoning of those years remains a matter to be stated modestly.

verses.text: For I know the thoughts that I think toward you,” says the LORD, “thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you hope and a future.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For I know the thoughts that I think toward you,” says the LORD, “thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you hope and a future.” The thoughts are the LORD’s toward these captives, in the same breath as the seventy years and the return. They are thoughts of peace, not of evil, to give that community hope and a future. The line should be kept in that setting. It is not a modern personal slogan; the caution can be spoken quietly, without scolding those who have drawn comfort from the words. Classical Arminians, here as elsewhere, affirm that God truly knows what he thinks and purposes, not that the future is open or unknown to him.

Arminian readers therefore take the verse as a real word of peace to the exiles, a future after the term of captivity, which they are invited to hope in as the LORD’s own thought toward them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear the LORD’s known thoughts toward this people: peace, not evil, hope and a future, bound to the promised visit and return after seventy years.

Shared ground: the words belong to the captives in Babylon and to that promised future. Both traditions can honor the comfort without lifting the verse out of the letter.

verses.text: You shall call on me, and you shall go and pray to me, and I will listen to you.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You shall call on me, and you shall go and pray to me, and I will listen to you.” Calling, going, and praying are met with the LORD’s listening. The promise stands in the letter’s hope of return, not as a detached rule about prayer in general. On how prayer relates to what God does, the existing box at Joshua 10:14 may be consulted; that discussion is not restated here.

Arminian readers hear a genuine invitation and a genuine promise to listen, given to a people who will call and pray, as the next verse will also say of seeking with all the heart.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same three acts and the promise “I will listen to you” as the LORD’s appointed way for these exiles, a listening he himself pledges. The existing box at Joshua 10:14 may be consulted and is not restated here.

Shared ground: they will pray, and he will listen. The traditions need not reopen the prayer question in this note.

verses.text: You shall seek me and find me, when you search for me with all your heart.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You shall seek me and find me, when you search for me with all your heart.” Seeking and finding are joined to searching with all the heart. The promise is still to this people, in the same movement as the call to pray and the hope of return. The existing box at Joshua 10:14 remains the place to consult on prayer and God’s purpose, and is not restated here.

Arminian readers take the “when” as a real condition the people are called to meet: all-heart searching, with a promised finding, not an empty invitation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same promise as the LORD’s: they will find him when they search with all their heart, a seeking he here binds to being found.

Shared ground: wholehearted search and promised finding belong together in this word to the exiles. The verse is comfort and call, not a new contrast.

verses.text: I will be found by you,” says the LORD, “and I will turn again your captivity, and I will gather you from all the nations, and from all the places where I have driven you,” says the LORD. “I will bring you again to the place from where I caused you to be carried away captive.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will be found by you,” says the LORD, “and I will turn again your captivity, and I will gather you from all the nations, and from all the places where I have driven you,” and “I will bring you again to the place from where I caused you to be carried away captive.” Being found is joined to a turning of captivity, a gathering from nations and places, and a bringing back to the place they left. The horizon is wider than one city of exile, though the letter is sent to Babylon.

Arminian readers hear a real restoration promised, a gathering they may hope in after the seventy years, as the LORD’s own finding and bringing back, not as a slogan detached from return.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same verbs as the LORD’s work: he will be found, turn the captivity, gather from all the nations and places, and bring them again to the place of their carrying-away.

Shared ground: the letter’s hope ends in return and gathering. Daniel 9:2, 2 Chronicles 36:21, and Ezra 1:1 may be compared later by reference, without a blended timetable here.
